Q: How do I store data that can be structured or non-structured at the same time? A:

We had the same requirement: the same kind of fact (e.g. an examination) sometimes arrives as narrative text and sometimes as structured fields. Duplicating it in two places (PATIENT blob + child table) felt wrong because it invites drift and awkward “union two shapes” queries.

What worked for us: treat one examination = one row in a dedicated medical_examination table, with both structured columns and a free-text column on that row:

  • Columns such as name, performed_on, result, etc. — all nullable.

  • A free_text (or notes) column for the narrative when we don’t have (or don’t yet have) structured fields.

Rule: for a given row, we either fill the structured fields or rely on free_text for the main content (sometimes we allow structured fields plus notes for extra commentary — that’s a product decision, but we avoid two competing full descriptions).

Why this is cleaner than two tables for “the same” information:

  • One place to insert/update per examination.

  • Listing “all examinations for a patient” is a single SELECT with optional COALESCE/CONCAT to build a display string when you need a uniform line in a report.

  • You can migrate over time: legacy = free_text only; new = structured; optional ETL from text to columns without maintaining parallel tables forever.

Caveats: you usually cannot make every structured column NOT NULL globally. Enforce “structured vs narrative” in the application, or with a CHECK constraint (e.g. require that either free_text is non-empty or key structured fields are present — whatever matches your policy).

Semi-structured fans can push the variable part into JSON/JSONB on the same row instead of many nullable columns; the mental model is the same: one row per exam, one optional blob for the irregular part.

This is in the same spirit as modeling “structured + comments” in one entity rather than splitting the same real-world object across two tables.

Q: Assigning colors to table values using choroplethr A:

Thank you for using Choroplethr.

I think that there are a few issues here. The first one I'd like to address is that your value column contains numeric data. This by itself is not a problem. But because you are actually using it to code categorical data (i.e. "MD", "OD", etc.) this is a problem. Therefore my first task will be to change the data type from numeric to character data:

> class(Res$value)
[1] "numeric"
> Res$value = as.character(Res$value)
> class(Res$value)
[1] "character"

Now I will replace the "numbers" with the category names that you want:

> Res[Res=="0"] = "None"
> Res[Res=="1"] = "MD"
> Res[Res=="2"] = "DO"
> Res[Res=="3"] = "Both"
> head(Res)
  region value
1  45001  None
2  22001    MD
3  51001    DO
4  16001  Both
5  19001  None
6  21001    MD

Now for the second issue. You said that you were trying to use scale_fill_brewer. That function is for using the Brewer scales. But you don't want those here. You say that you have your own scale. So you want to use scale_fill_manual. 

county_choropleth(Res) + 
  scale_fill_manual(values=c("None" = "#ffffffff",  
                             "MD" = "#64acbe", 
                             "DO" = "#c85a5a", 
                             "Both" = "#574249"),
                    name="Types of Medical Residencies")

Note: What choroplethr calls the "legend" (which is actually the name of the legend) is actually a property of the ggplot2 scale. In particular, it is the name of the scale. So if you are using your own scale, you cannot use choroplethr's legend parameter any more.

Of course, now we have a new problem: Alaska and Hawaii are all black. I actually forgot about this issue (it's been a while since I worked on Choroplethr). The reason this happens is very technical, and perhaps more detailed than you care for, but I will mention it here for completeness: choroplethr uses ggplot2 annotations to render AK and HI in the proper place. the choropelthr + ggplot_scale paradigm does not work here for AK and HI because ggplot does not propogate additional layers / scales to annotations. To get around this we must use the object-oriented features of choroplethr:

c = CountyChoropleth$new(Res)
c$title = "All United States Medical Residencies"
c$ggplot_scale = scale_fill_manual(values=c("None" = "#ffffffff", "MD" = "#64acbe", "DO" = "#c85a5a", "Both" = "#574249"), 
                                   name="Types of Medical Residencies")
c$render()

Q: Exceeded max user connections in python / flask / mysql A:

The error 1226 is a MySQL Server error. This is definitely the result of your app connecting to the server.

Probably it makes 10 connections immediately as the Flask bootstraps, because that's the size of the pool.

Increasing your pool size will not help, since that will make more connections, and that will still exceed the server's per-user limit. The connection pool is in your client app, not in the server.

The error is related to per-user connection limits. That is, the MySQL Server may allow 151 (the default), but the error you got indicates that this given user is limited to 10 connections at a time. The max_user_connnections config option affects all users, or else any individual user can be granted a limited number of connections (see the MAX_USER_CONNECTIONS clause in ALTER USER).

You need to find out from your database administrator or cloud service provider why the max user connections limit is configured the way it is, and if it can be changed.

An alternative is to configure a connection pool in your app that is smaller than the limit.

If you have more than one instance of your app running, connecting to the same MySQL Server with the same user credentials, you'll again exceed the connection limit.

Q: How to use MAP() , BYCOL() or BYROW() to return multiple arrays? A:

The below formula is in cell H2 and spill the result.
The formula add a column with a sequenced number of rows in the table, then SORT, returns the sorted rows numbers and then create the table with TEXTJOIN and TEXTSPLIT functions.
All ranges in the formula are the table data (in sample data B2:E6) without the row/column titles.

=WRAPCOLS(TEXTSPLIT(TEXTJOIN("|",FALSE,BYCOL(B2:E6,LAMBDA(x,TEXTJOIN("|",FALSE,TAKE(SORT(HSTACK(x,SEQUENCE(ROWS(B2:E6))),1),,-1))))),"|"),ROWS(B2:E6))

EDIT
Thanks for @rotabor observation the edited formula works with tables of different row and column count.

Q: SQLite isn't getting installed in Docker A:

It might be that the Node image doesn't include SQLite.

To confirm, start your app with docker-compose up -d to start the container in detached mode. Use the exec command to open Bash in your container to access the container's command line, then run which sqlite3 in your container to confirm you do not have it installed:

$ docker-compose up -d
$ docker-compose exec backend /bin/bash
$ which sqlite3
$ exit

If running which sqlite3 returns no output, then you don't have SQLite installed in your container. It was working in Windows because it's installed on the OS. To fix this, you'll need to install SQLite in your Dockerfile on line 4:

RUN apt update && apt install -y apt-transport-https ca-certificates

Dockerfile line 4 updated:

RUN apt update && apt install -y apt-transport-https ca-certificates sqlite3
